claims.claim: rBLA primarily activates PL L2 in vivo.
claims.source: We next combined in vivo silicon probe recordings and optogenetics to confirm that cBLA mainly influences IL L5, whereas rBLA primarily activates PL L2, but also evokes polysynaptic activity in PL L5.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo Neuropixels recordings with optogenetic stimulation shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: rBLA evokes polysynaptic activity in PL L5.
claims.source: We next combined in vivo silicon probe recordings and optogenetics to confirm that cBLA mainly influences IL L5, whereas rBLA primarily activates PL L2, but also evokes polysynaptic activity in PL L5.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4 and ex vivo recordings shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: rBLA can engage L2 CA neurons to impact L5 PT neuron activity.
claims.source: Lastly, we used soma-tagged optogenetics to explore the local circuits linking superficial and deep layers of PL, showing how rBLA can engage L2 CA neurons to impact L5 PT neuron activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by soma-tagged optogenetics experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claims.claim: The BLA sends strong excitatory inputs to the PFC.
claims.source: The BLA sends strong excitatory inputs to the PFC, which contact specific cell types to drive local activity and output to downstream brain areas (Sotres-Bayon et al., 2012; Little and Carter, 2013; Cheriyan et al., 2016; Burgos-Robles et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: BLA inputs contact specific cell types in the PFC to drive local activity and output to downstream brain areas.
claims.source: The BLA sends strong excitatory inputs to the PFC, which contact specific cell types to drive local activity and output to downstream brain areas (Sotres-Bayon et al., 2012; Little and Carter, 2013; Cheriyan et al., 2016; Burgos-Robles et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The PFC is subdivided along the dorsoventral axis into the prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) regions.
claims.source: The PFC is subdivided along the dorsoventral axis into the prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) regions (Van De Werd et al., 2010; Van De Werd and Uylings, 2014), which play different functional roles in behavioral paradigms like threat conditioning (Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: PL and IL play different functional roles in behavioral paradigms like threat conditioning.
claims.source: The PFC is subdivided along the dorsoventral axis into the prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) regions (Van De Werd et al., 2010; Van De Werd and Uylings, 2014), which play different functional roles in behavioral paradigms like threat conditioning (Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The BLA is subdivided along the rostro-caudal axis into anterior (magnocellular) and posterior (parvocellular) regions.
claims.source: Similarly, the BLA is subdivided along the rostro-caudal axis into anterior (magnocellular) and posterior (parvocellular) regions (McDonald, 2003; O'Leary et al., 2020), which also play distinct roles in aversive and appetitive behaviors (Kim et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Anterior and posterior regions of the BLA play distinct roles in aversive and appetitive behaviors.
claims.source: Similarly, the BLA is subdivided along the rostro-caudal axis into anterior (magnocellular) and posterior (parvocellular) regions (McDonald, 2003; O'Leary et al., 2020), which also play distinct roles in aversive and appetitive behaviors (Kim et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: One population of cells in anterior BLA targets PL, while a separate group in posterior BLA targets IL.
claims.source: Anatomical studies using transgenic mice suggest one population of cells in anterior BLA targets PL, while a separate group in posterior BLA targets IL (Kim et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: There are multiple projections from cells distributed along the rostral to caudal axis of the BLA.
claims.source: However, recent work suggests a more complicated relationship, with multiple projections from cells distributed along the rostral to caudal axis of the BLA (Hintiryan et al., 2021), which have an unknown influence on activity and output of the PFC.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: BLA inputs to PL target layer 2 (L2) cortico-amygdalar (CA) neurons.
claims.source: BLA inputs to PL target layer 2 (L2) cortico-amygdalar (CA) neurons, which in turn project back to the BLA, forming a direct, reciprocal circuit under the control of local inhibition (Little and Carter, 2013; McGarry and Carter, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: PL L2 CA neurons project back to the BLA, forming a direct, reciprocal circuit under the control of local inhibition.
claims.source: BLA inputs to PL target layer 2 (L2) cortico-amygdalar (CA) neurons, which in turn project back to the BLA, forming a direct, reciprocal circuit under the control of local inhibition (Little and Carter, 2013; McGarry and Carter, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: BLA connections in IL can activate layer 5 (L5) pyramidal tract (PT) neurons.
claims.source: In contrast, BLA connections in IL can activate layer 5 (L5) pyramidal tract (PT) neurons, which project to the periaqueductal gray (PAG) and other brain regions to exert top-down control of behavior (Cheriyan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: IL L5 PT neurons project to the periaqueductal gray (PAG) and other brain regions to exert top-down control of behavior.
claims.source: In contrast, BLA connections in IL can activate layer 5 (L5) pyramidal tract (PT) neurons, which project to the periaqueductal gray (PAG) and other brain regions to exert top-down control of behavior (Cheriyan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Largely separate populations of PL and IL-projecting neurons exist across the BLA.
claims.source: We observed largely separate populations of PL and IL-projecting neurons across the BLA, with a smaller population of dual-projection neurons (PL = 583 ± 59 cells, IL = 694 ± 78 cells, dual = 246 ± 30 cells, n = 3 animals) (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: PL-projecting neurons are biased toward the rostral BLA (rBLA).
claims.source: Labeled cells were distributed along a gradient in the rostro-caudal axis, with PL-projecting neurons biased toward the rostral BLA (rBLA), and IL-projecting neurons shifted toward the cBLA (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: IL-projecting neurons are shifted toward the cBLA.
claims.source: Labeled cells were distributed along a gradient in the rostro-caudal axis, with PL-projecting neurons biased toward the rostral BLA (rBLA), and IL-projecting neurons shifted toward the cBLA (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: rBLA axons are primarily in PL and cBLA axons are in IL.
claims.source: Consistent with our retrograde labeling, we observed rBLA axons primarily in PL and cBLA axons in IL, with distinct laminar targeting in each subregion (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from anterograde tracing shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: rBLA primarily targets PL L2.
claims.source: Quantifying axon fluorescence across layers and subregions established that rBLA primarily targeted PL L2, whereas cBLA targeted IL L5 (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from anterograde tracing shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: cBLA targets IL L5.
claims.source: Quantifying axon fluorescence across layers and subregions established that rBLA primarily targeted PL L2, whereas cBLA targeted IL L5 (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from anterograde tracing shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: rBLA-evoked EPSCs are much larger at PL L2 CA neurons compared to IL L2 CA, PL L5 PT, and IL L5 PT neurons.
claims.source: Taking this approach, we observed that rBLA-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) at −60 mV were much larger at PL L2 CA neurons compared to all other cell types in the different layers and subregions (EPSC ratio: IL L2 CA vs. PL L2 CA = 0.03, geometric standard deviation factor [GSD] = 12.3, p = 0.0003; n = 8 pairs; PL L5 PT vs. PL L2 CA = 0.02, GSD = 2.6, p = 0.0001; n = 8 pairs; IL L5 PT vs. PL L2 CA = 0.09, GSD = 7.7, p = 0.006; n = 8 pairs; 5 animals) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: cBLA-evoked EPSCs are much larger at IL L5 PT neurons compared to PL L2 CA, IL L2 CA, and PL L5 PT neurons.
claims.source: In contrast, cBLA-evoked EPSCs were much larger at IL L5 PT neurons compared to all other cell types (EPSC ratio: PL L2 CA vs. IL L5 PT = 0.06, GSD = 9.3, p = 0.005; n = 7 pairs; IL L2 CA vs. IL L5 PT = 0.11, GSD = 10.5, p = 0.014; n = 7 pairs; PL L5 PT vs. IL L5 PT = 0.008, GSD = 3.1, p < 0.0001; n = 8 pairs; 6 animals) (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: rBLA and cBLA primarily make connections close to the soma of pyramidal neurons in the PFC.
claims.source: We found strong rBLA and cBLA input to the basal and perisomatic dendrites of PL L2 CA and IL L5 PT neurons, respectively, and no rBLA input to either the apical or basal dendrites of PL L5 PT neurons (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from subcellular channelrhodopsin-assisted circuit mapping (sCRACM) shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: rBLA does not target the apical or basal dendrites of PL L5 PT neurons.
claims.source: We found strong rBLA and cBLA input to the basal and perisomatic dendrites of PL L2 CA and IL L5 PT neurons, respectively, and no rBLA input to either the apical or basal dendrites of PL L5 PT neurons (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from sCRACM shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: rBLA-evoked EPSCs are largest at PL L2 CA neurons compared to IL L5 PT neurons.
claims.source: We found that rBLA-evoked EPSCs were again largest at PL L2 CA neurons (EPSC1: PL L2 CA = −401 ± 63 pA; IL L5 PT = −133 ± 55 pA; PL L2 CA vs. IL L5 PT, p = 0.0078, n = 8 pairs, 5 animals) (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: rBLA-evoked IPSCs are of comparable amplitude at PL L2 CA and IL L5 PT neurons.
claims.source: In contrast, rBLA-evoked IPSCs were of comparable amplitude at PL L2 CA and IL L5 PT neurons (IPSC1: PL L2 CA = 450 ± 86 pA; IL L5 PT = 521 ± 136 pA; PL L2 CA vs. IL L5 PT, p = 0.8125, n = 7 pairs, 5 animals) (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: rBLA inputs onto PL L2 CA neurons show higher E/I ratios than IL L5 PT neurons.
claims.source: We found differences in excitation/inhibition (E/I) ratios, with rBLA inputs onto PL L2 CA neurons showing higher values than IL L5 PT neurons (rBLA E/I ratio: PL L2 CA = 0.99, GSD = 1.9; IL L5 PT = 0.15, GSD = 2.7; PL L2 CA vs. IL L5 PT, p = 0.0156, n = 7 pairs, 5 animals) (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: cBLA-evoked EPSCs and IPSCs are strongly biased onto IL L5 PT neurons compared to PL L2 CA neurons.
claims.source: We found that both EPSCs and IPSCs were strongly biased onto IL L5 PT neurons (EPSC1: PL L2 CA = −31 ± 10 pA; IL L5 PT = −415 ± 139 pA; PL L2 CA vs. IL L5 PT, p = 0.0156, n = 7 pairs, 4 animals) (IPSC1: PL L2 CA = 31 ± 28 pA; IL L5 PT = 858 ± 149 pA; PL L2 CA vs. IL L5 PT, p = 0.0156, n = 7 pairs, 4 animals) (cBLA E/I ratio; IL L5 PT = 0.4, GSD = 2.3; n = 7 pairs, 4 animals) (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: rBLA inputs evoke significantly more action potential firing of PL L2 CA neurons compared to IL L5 PT neurons.
claims.source: We found that rBLA inputs evoked significantly more action potential firing of PL L2 CA neurons compared to IL L5 PT neurons in the same slices (firing probability: PL L2 CA = 0.88 ± 0.05, IL L5 PT = 0.23 ± 0.15, p = 0.016; n = 8 pairs, 5 animals) (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: cBLA inputs activate only IL L5 PT neurons and never activate PL L2 CA neurons.
claims.source: In contrast, cBLA inputs activated only IL L5 PT neurons and never activated PL L2 CA neurons (firing probability: PL L2 CA = 0, IL L5 PT = 0.98 ± 0.02, p = 0.03; n = 7 pairs, 3 animals) (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: rBLA stimulation leads to more responsive units in PL L2, PL L5, and IL L5 compared to IL L2.
claims.source: rBLA stimulation led to more responsive units in PL L2, PL L5, and IL L5 compared to IL L2 (PL L2 = 20.1%; IL L2 = 9.8%; PL L5 = 20.0%; IL L5 = 23.9% of single units in subregion), whereas cBLA stimulation mainly drove responses in IL L5 (PL L2 = 2.6%; IL L2 = 7.5%; PL L5 = 12.9%; IL L5 = 26.6% of single units in subregion) (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: cBLA stimulation mainly drives responses in IL L5.
claims.source: rBLA stimulation led to more responsive units in PL L2, PL L5, and IL L5 compared to IL L2 (PL L2 = 20.1%; IL L2 = 9.8%; PL L5 = 20.0%; IL L5 = 23.9% of single units in subregion), whereas cBLA stimulation mainly drove responses in IL L5 (PL L2 = 2.6%; IL L2 = 7.5%; PL L5 = 12.9%; IL L5 = 26.6% of single units in subregion) (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The highest proportion of rBLA-activated units are found in PL L2.
claims.source: The highest proportion of rBLA-activated units were found in PL L2 (PL L2 = 18.2%; IL L2 = 5.5%; PL L5 = 7.9%; IL L5 = 9.9% of single units in subregion), whereas rBLA-suppressed units were enriched in L5 of PL and IL (PL L2 = 1.9%; IL L2 = 4.3%; PL L5 = 12.4%; IL L5 = 14% of single units in subregion) (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: rBLA-suppressed units are enriched in L5 of PL and IL.
claims.source: The highest proportion of rBLA-activated units were found in PL L2 (PL L2 = 18.2%; IL L2 = 5.5%; PL L5 = 7.9%; IL L5 = 9.9% of single units in subregion), whereas rBLA-suppressed units were enriched in L5 of PL and IL (PL L2 = 1.9%; IL L2 = 4.3%; PL L5 = 12.4%; IL L5 = 14% of single units in subregion) (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: cBLA-activated units are greatest in IL L5.
claims.source: In contrast, cBLA-activated units were greatest in IL L5 (PL L2 = 1.3%; IL L2 = 5%; PL L5 = 4%; IL L5 = 17.7% of single units in subregion), with no significant differences in the proportion of cBLA-suppressed units (PL L2 = 1.3%; IL L2 = 2.5%; PL L5 = 8.9%; IL L5 = 8.9% of single units in subregion) (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: rBLA evokes robust responses at PL L5 PT neurons at suprathreshold intensities but not at subthreshold intensities.
claims.source: We found no responses at subthreshold intensities, but robust responses at suprathreshold intensities, suggesting polysynaptic activity from L2 to L5 is involved in rBLA-evoked responses at PL L5 PT neurons (EPSC: sub = −9 ± 4 pA, supra = −113 ± 24 pA, p = 0.02; n = 8 pairs; IPSC: sub = 17 ± 5 pA, supra = 508 ± 101 pA, p = 0.008; n = 8 pairs; 4 animals) (Figure 5B, C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: Polysynaptic activity from L2 to L5 is involved in rBLA-evoked responses at PL L5 PT neurons.
claims.source: We found no responses at subthreshold intensities, but robust responses at suprathreshold intensities, suggesting polysynaptic activity from L2 to L5 is involved in rBLA-evoked responses at PL L5 PT neurons (EPSC: sub = −9 ± 4 pA, supra = −113 ± 24 pA, p = 0.02; n = 8 pairs; IPSC: sub = 17 ± 5 pA, supra = 508 ± 101 pA, p = 0.008; n = 8 pairs; 4 animals) (Figure 5B, C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 5B and 5C, and by inference from the lack of monosynaptic connections.

claims.claim: rBLA does not evoke responses in IL L5 PT neurons at either subthreshold or suprathreshold intensities.
claims.source: In contrast, we observed no responses in IL L5 PT neurons at either subthreshold or suprathreshold intensities, suggesting activity does not spread from PL L2 to IL L5 in the slice, and that rBLA instead projects directly to IL L5 (EPSC: sub = −4 ± 3 pA, supra = −7 ± 4 pA, p = 0.055; n = 8 pairs; IPSC: sub = −7 ± 2 pA, supra = −11 ± 3 pA, p = 0.64; n = 8 pairs; 3 animals) (Figure 5D–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 5D-F.

claims.claim: Activity does not spread from PL L2 to IL L5 in the slice.
claims.source: In contrast, we observed no responses in IL L5 PT neurons at either subthreshold or suprathreshold intensities, suggesting activity does not spread from PL L2 to IL L5 in the slice, and that rBLA instead projects directly to IL L5 (EPSC: sub = −4 ± 3 pA, supra = −7 ± 4 pA, p = 0.055; n = 8 pairs; IPSC: sub = −7 ± 2 pA, supra = −11 ± 3 pA, p = 0.64; n = 8 pairs; 3 animals) (Figure 5D–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 5D-F and by inference from the lack of responses.

claims.claim: cBLA does not engage PL L5 via IL L5.
claims.source: In order to confirm that cBLA does not engage PL L5 via IL L5, we also activated cBLA inputs in IL L5, and observed no EPSCs in PL L5 PT neurons at either subthreshold or suprathreshold intensities, and only minimal IPSCs at suprathreshold intensities, suggesting polysynaptic activity also does not spread from IL L5 to PL L5 (EPSC: sub = −4 ± 2 pA, supra = −13 ± 5 pA, p = 0.055; n = 9 pairs; IPSC: sub = 7 ± 2 pA, supra = 54 ± 22 pA, p = 0.027; n = 9 pairs; 3 animals) (Figure 5G–I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 5G-I.

claims.claim: Polysynaptic activity does not spread from IL L5 to PL L5.
claims.source: In order to confirm that cBLA does not engage PL L5 via IL L5, we also activated cBLA inputs in IL L5, and observed no EPSCs in PL L5 PT neurons at either subthreshold or suprathreshold intensities, and only minimal IPSCs at suprathreshold intensities, suggesting polysynaptic activity also does not spread from IL L5 to PL L5 (EPSC: sub = −4 ± 2 pA, supra = −13 ± 5 pA, p = 0.055; n = 9 pairs; IPSC: sub = 7 ± 2 pA, supra = 54 ± 22 pA, p = 0.027; n = 9 pairs; 3 animals) (Figure 5G–I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figure 5G-I and by inference from the lack of responses.

claims.claim: L2 stimulation can exclusively drive L2 CA neurons without engaging L5 CA neurons.
claims.source: We found that L2 stimulation could exclusively drive L2 CA neurons without engaging L5 CA neurons, whereas L5 stimulation could drive L5 CA neurons without engaging L2 CA neurons, demonstrating restricted layer-specific activation (Figure 6C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claims.claim: L5 stimulation can drive L5 CA neurons without engaging L2 CA neurons.
claims.source: We found that L2 stimulation could exclusively drive L2 CA neurons without engaging L5 CA neurons, whereas L5 stimulation could drive L5 CA neurons without engaging L2 CA neurons, demonstrating restricted layer-specific activation (Figure 6C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claims.claim: PL L2 CA neurons evoke prominent EPSCs at L2 and L5 pyramidal neurons, but minimal responses at L3 pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: We found prominent EPSCs at L2 and L5 pyramidal neurons, but minimal responses at L3 pyramidal neurons (EPSC: L2 Pyr = −61 ± 19 pA, L3 Pyr = –13 ± 3 pA, L5 Pyr = −237 ± 96 pA; L2 vs. L3, p = 0.0373; L3 vs. L5, p = 0.0014; n = 8 triplets; 4 animals) (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: PL L2 CA neurons evoke prominent inhibition at L2 and L5 pyramidal neurons, with minimal responses at L3 pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: We also observed prominent inhibition at L2 and L5 pyramidal neurons, again with minimal responses at L3 pyramidal neurons (IPSC: L2 Pyr = 888 ± 263 pA, L3 Pyr = 80 ± 56 pA, L5 Pyr = 449 ± 236 pA; L2 vs. L3, p = 0.0014; n = 8 triplets; 4 animals) (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: L5 pyramidal neurons have a significantly higher E/I ratio compared to L2 and L3 pyramidal neurons.
claims.source: The overall effect was a significantly higher E/I ratio at L5 pyramidal neurons compared to the other cell types (E/I ratio: L2 Pyr = 0.06, GSD = 1.8, L3 Pyr = 0.36, GSD = 5.5, L5 Pyr = 0.8, GSD = 2.8; L2 vs. L5, p = 0.0059; n = 7 L2, 5 L3, and 8 L5 cells; 4 animals).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics.

claims.claim: PL L2 CA-evoked EPSCs and IPSCs are strongly biased onto L5 PT neurons compared to neighboring L5 IT neurons.
claims.source: We observed robust PL L2 CA-evoked EPSCs and IPSCs, which were strongly biased onto L5 PT neurons compared to neighboring L5 IT neurons (EPSC: PL L5 PT = −67 ± 15 pA, PL L5 IT = −4 ± 1 pA, p = 0.0005; n = 12 pairs; 7 animals; IPSC: PL L5 PT = 229 ± 92 pA, PL L5 IT = 20 ± 15 pA, p = 0.03; n = 10 pairs; 6 animals) (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Excitatory conductances alone evoke robust spiking in L5 PT neurons but not L5 IT neurons.
claims.source: We found that excitatory conductances alone evoked robust spiking in L5 PT neurons but not L5 IT neurons, whereas injecting excitatory and inhibitory conductances resulted in significantly attenuated spiking of PT neurons (spikes per stimulus: PT E = 6.82 ± 0.54; PT E + I = 1.07 ± 0.49; IT E = 0 ± 0; IT E + I = 0 ± 0; n = 7 for each cell type, 4 animals) (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from dynamic-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Injecting excitatory and inhibitory conductances results in significantly attenuated spiking of PT neurons.
claims.source: We found that excitatory conductances alone evoked robust spiking in L5 PT neurons but not L5 IT neurons, whereas injecting excitatory and inhibitory conductances resulted in significantly attenuated spiking of PT neurons (spikes per stimulus: PT E = 6.82 ± 0.54; PT E + I = 1.07 ± 0.49; IT E = 0 ± 0; IT E + I = 0 ± 0; n = 7 for each cell type, 4 animals) (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from dynamic-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Activation of PL L2 CA neurons drives PL L5 PT spiking, but this can be strongly regulated by local inhibitory circuits.
claims.source: These results indicate that activation of PL L2 CA neurons drives PL L5 PT spiking, but this can be strongly regulated by local inhibitory circuits.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from dynamic-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7D and by inference from the E/I balance experiments.

claims.claim: rBLA primarily projects to PL and cBLA mostly projects to IL, indicating distinct connections.
claims.source: We first use anatomy to show that rBLA primarily projects to PL, and cBLA mostly projects to IL, indicating distinct connections.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde and anterograde tracing shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: rBLA preferentially activates PL L2 CA neurons and cBLA engages IL L5 PT neurons.
claims.source: We next use ex vivo recordings and optogenetics to assess cell type-specific connections, showing that rBLA preferentially activates PL L2 CA neurons and cBLA engages IL L5 PT neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo electrophysiology shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claims.claim: cBLA influences are restricted to IL L5.
claims.source: We then combine in vivo recordings with optogenetics and find that while cBLA influences are restricted to IL L5, rBLA drives both PL L2 and evokes robust polysynaptic activity in PL L5.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: rBLA drives both PL L2 and evokes robust polysynaptic activity in PL L5.
claims.source: We then combine in vivo recordings with optogenetics and find that while cBLA influences are restricted to IL L5, rBLA drives both PL L2 and evokes robust polysynaptic activity in PL L5.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo Neuropixels recordings shown in Figure 4 and ex vivo recordings shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: PL L2 CA neurons mediate polysynaptic responses at PL L5 PT neurons.
claims.source: Lastly, using soma-tagged optogenetics, we establish that this local influence reflects connections from PL L2 CA neurons onto PL L5 PT neurons within PL.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soma-tagged optogenetics shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claims.claim: Dysfunction of BLA-PFC connections contributes to neuropsychiatric disorders, including post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, and autism.
claims.source: Dysfunction of these connections contributes to neuropsychiatric disorders, including post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, and autism (Gilboa et al., 2004; Felix-Ortiz et al., 2016; McTeague et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Long-range inputs often make targeted connections onto specific cell types in the PFC.
claims.source: In addition to contacting different subregions and layers, long-range inputs often make targeted connections onto specific cell types in the PFC (Anastasiades and Carter, 2021).

claims.claim: PL-projecting neurons in rBLA and IL-projecting neurons in cBLA do not collateralize within PFC.

results.result: rBLA and cBLA form anatomically distinct projections to PL and IL subregions of the PFC. Retrograde tracing shows PL-projecting neurons are biased toward rBLA while IL-projecting neurons are shifted toward cBLA. Anterograde tracing confirms rBLA axons primarily target PL L2 while cBLA axons target IL L5, with minimal collateralization within PFC.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C22-C27, C58, and C67 are well-supported by converging anatomical evidence from both retrograde and anterograde tracing experiments (Figure 1 and supplements). The quantitative data on cell distributions and axonal fluorescence across layers provide strong anatomical evidence for distinct rBLA→PL and cBLA→IL projections. The retrograde-Cre experiments (C67) further confirm lack of collateralization.

results.result: rBLA preferentially drives PL L2 CA neurons while cBLA drives IL L5 PT neurons through cell type-specific monosynaptic connections. Ex vivo recordings with optogenetics show rBLA-evoked EPSCs are much larger at PL L2 CA neurons compared to other cell types, while cBLA-evoked EPSCs are much larger at IL L5 PT neurons. sCRACM mapping reveals these connections target perisomatic/basal dendrites rather than apical dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C28-C31, C59, C68-C71 are strongly supported by ex vivo electrophysiology with optogenetics (Figures 2-3). The use of TTX+4-AP to isolate monosynaptic connections is appropriate, and the large differences in EPSC amplitudes (10-100 fold) with statistical significance provide robust evidence. sCRACM data (C30-C31) adds subcellular resolution. The cell type specificity is confirmed across multiple complementary experiments.

results.result: rBLA and cBLA inputs evoke distinct patterns of excitation and inhibition that drive cell type-specific firing in PFC. rBLA inputs show higher E/I ratios at PL L2 CA neurons and evoke significantly more action potential firing compared to IL L5 PT neurons. In contrast, cBLA inputs strongly bias both EPSCs and IPSCs onto IL L5 PT neurons and activate only these neurons, never activating PL L2 CA neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C37, C72-C74 are well-supported by ex vivo recordings under more physiological conditions (Figure 3). The paired recordings control for slice-to-slice variability, and the measurements of both EPSCs and IPSCs at physiological holding potentials provide comprehensive characterization. The E/I ratio differences and firing probability data (C36-C37) demonstrate functional consequences. Statistical significance is reported throughout.

results.result: In vivo Neuropixels recordings confirm that cBLA mainly influences IL L5 while rBLA primarily activates PL L2 but also generates mixed activation and suppression across L5. rBLA stimulation leads to the highest proportion of activated units in PL L2 (18.2%) with suppressed units enriched in L5 of both PL and IL. cBLA-activated units are greatest in IL L5 (17.7%) with few responses elsewhere.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C38-C42, C60, C75-C77 are supported by in vivo Neuropixels recordings (Figure 4). The use of awake, head-fixed mice provides physiological relevance. Statistical tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank, chi-squared with Holm-Bonferroni correction) are appropriate. The layer and subregion assignments using Allen CCF registration add rigor. However, the lack of significant latency differences between PL L2 and PL L5 activated units (noted in text) is somewhat unexpected given the polysynaptic nature proposed, though technical limitations are acknowledged.

results.result: rBLA evokes polysynaptic activity in PL L5 PT neurons via local circuits. Subthreshold rBLA stimulation that does not activate PL L2 CA neurons evokes no responses in PL L5 PT neurons, while suprathreshold stimulation evokes robust EPSCs and IPSCs. Activity does not spread from PL L2 to IL L5 or from IL L5 to PL L5 in slices, and cBLA does not engage PL L5 via IL L5.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C43-C48, C61 are supported by ex vivo recordings with graded optogenetic stimulation (Figure 5). The experimental design using subthreshold vs suprathreshold stimulation intensities is appropriate for distinguishing monosynaptic from polysynaptic responses. The lack of responses at subthreshold intensities combined with robust responses at suprathreshold intensities (C43-C44) provides strong evidence for polysynaptic mechanisms. The negative results (C45-C48) are important controls showing specificity of the PL L2→PL L5 pathway.

results.result: PL L2 CA neurons mediate polysynaptic responses at PL L5 PT neurons through a disynaptic feedforward circuit. Soma-tagged optogenetics demonstrates layer-specific activation, with L2 stimulation driving L2 CA neurons without engaging L5 CA neurons. PL L2 CA neurons evoke prominent EPSCs and IPSCs at L2 and L5 pyramidal neurons but minimal responses at L3, with L5 pyramidal neurons showing significantly higher E/I ratios. These responses are strongly biased onto L5 PT neurons compared to L5 IT neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C49-C54, C62, C78-C79 are well-supported by soma-tagged optogenetics experiments (Figures 6-7). The use of st-ChroME provides spatial specificity confirmed by control experiments (C49-C50). The layer-specific connectivity pattern (C51-C53) with statistical significance demonstrates the L2→L5 pathway while bypassing L3. The cell type-specific targeting of L5 PT over L5 IT neurons (C54) is robustly demonstrated with significant differences in both EPSCs and IPSCs.

results.result: Activation of PL L2 CA neurons drives PL L5 PT spiking through excitatory conductances, but this can be strongly regulated by local inhibitory circuits. Dynamic-clamp recordings show excitatory conductances alone evoke robust spiking in L5 PT neurons but not L5 IT neurons, while injecting both excitatory and inhibitory conductances results in significantly attenuated spiking of PT neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by dynamic-clamp experiments (Figure 7D). The approach of injecting scaled conductances derived from voltage-clamp recordings is appropriate for assessing functional impact. The differential effects on PT vs IT neurons and the attenuation by inhibition are clearly demonstrated with statistical significance. However, the dynamic-clamp approach makes assumptions about conductance kinetics and spatial integration that may not fully capture in vivo dynamics.

results.result: BLA-PFC connections regulate memory and emotion and become disrupted in neuropsychiatric disorders including PTSD, depression, and autism. The BLA sends strong excitatory inputs to the PFC that contact specific cell types to drive local activity and output to downstream brain areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C11, C63 are supported by citations to prior literature. These are well-established background claims that provide context for the current study. The citations appear appropriate for these general statements about BLA-PFC function and dysfunction.

results.result: The PFC is subdivided into PL and IL regions that play different functional roles, and the BLA is subdivided into anterior and posterior regions that also play distinct roles in behavior. Prior anatomical studies suggest anterior BLA targets PL while posterior BLA targets IL, though recent work suggests more complex projections. BLA inputs to PL target L2 CA neurons forming reciprocal circuits, while BLA connections in IL activate L5 PT neurons that project to subcortical regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C21 are supported by citations to prior literature. These background claims establish the anatomical and functional organization of PFC and BLA subregions and summarize prior findings on BLA-PFC connectivity. The citations appear appropriate and provide necessary context for the current study's hypotheses.

results.result: Long-range inputs often make targeted connections onto specific cell types in the PFC. In motor cortex, L2/3 neurons project to deeper layers and target L5 pyramidal neurons, whereas L5 PT neurons predominantly target nearby L5 PT neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by citations to prior literature. These provide relevant background on cell type-specific connectivity and translaminar projections in cortex, which inform the hypotheses and interpretation of the current study.

results.result: The influence of rBLA on PFC output will depend on the neuromodulatory state, which may alter the tightly balanced CA-evoked excitation and inhibition onto PL L5 PT neurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is speculative and based on inference from the E/I balance experiments combined with citations to prior literature on neuromodulation. While the E/I balance data (C55-C57) support that inhibition can regulate PT neuron firing, the claim about neuromodulatory state dependence is not directly tested in this study. This represents a reasonable hypothesis for future work but lacks direct experimental support.

results.result: rBLA participates in a closed reciprocal loop with PL, contacting L2 CA neurons that project back to rBLA, while cBLA does not participate in a closed or open reciprocal loop with IL, instead making unidirectional connections onto L5 PT neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 are supported by the current experimental data combined with prior literature. C81 is confirmed by the current findings showing rBLA targets PL L2 CA neurons, combined with prior work (Little and Carter, 2013) showing these neurons project back to BLA. C82 is supported by data showing cBLA targets IL L5 PT neurons (which do not project to BLA based on Figure 5—figure supplement 1) rather than IL L5 CA neurons.

results.result: BLA to PL projections are necessary for expression of threat conditioning, and rBLA plays a key role in aversion. BLA to IL projections are involved in extinction of threat conditioning, and cBLA is involved in this learning. Recent work suggests neurons encoding both positive and negative valence exist within rBLA, meaning both PL and IL could receive signals encoding positive and negative valence from different BLA sources.
results.evaluation: Claims C83, C85, C87 are supported by citations to prior literature. Claims C84, C86, C88 involve inference from the current study's anatomical findings combined with prior behavioral literature. The inferences are reasonable given that rBLA is the main input to PL and cBLA is the main input to IL, but the functional roles are not directly tested behaviorally in this study. These represent well-supported interpretations of how the current anatomical findings relate to prior behavioral work.

results.result: Subregions of the BLA target distinct networks within the PFC and differentially influence output from PL and IL. rBLA and cBLA evoke activity in PL and IL, demonstrating how subregions of the BLA engage distinct cortical networks in the PFC.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 are overarching conclusions supported by the comprehensive experimental data from all experiments in the study. These summary claims integrate findings from anatomy (C3, C22-C27), ex vivo physiology (C4-C5, C28-C37), in vivo recordings (C6-C7, C38-C42), and local circuit mapping (C9, C49-C57). The evidence converges to support these main conclusions.
